claim: Several human studies have found peaks in neural activity preceding voluntary actions, for example the readiness potential (RP).
source: Several human studies have found peaks in neural activity preceding voluntary actions, for example the readiness potential (RP), and some have shown upcoming actions could be decoded even before awareness.
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on the readiness potential in human voluntary action studies.

claim: Some human studies have shown upcoming actions could be decoded even before awareness.
source: Several human studies have found peaks in neural activity preceding voluntary actions, for example the readiness potential (RP), and some have shown upcoming actions could be decoded even before awareness.
evidence: Supported by citations to human studies on decoding voluntary actions.

claim: Cortical activity changes in variance seconds prior to movement in mice performing self-initiated lever pulls.
source: Implementing a self-initiated water-rewarded lever-pull paradigm in mice while recording widefield [Ca++] neural activity we find that cortical activity changes in variance seconds prior to movement and that upcoming lever pulls could be predicted between 3 and 5 s (or more in some cases) prior to movement.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from widefield calcium imaging during self-initiated behavior.

claim: Upcoming lever pulls could be predicted between 3 and 5 s (or more in some cases) prior to movement.
source: Implementing a self-initiated water-rewarded lever-pull paradigm in mice while recording widefield [Ca++] neural activity we find that cortical activity changes in variance seconds prior to movement and that upcoming lever pulls could be predicted between 3 and 5 s (or more in some cases) prior to movement.
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis of neural activity preceding lever pulls.

claim: Inhibition of motor cortex starts at approximately 5 s prior to lever pulls.
source: We found inhibition of motor cortex starting at approximately 5 s prior to lever pulls and activation of motor cortex starting at approximately 2 s prior to a random unrewarded left limb movement.
evidence: Supported by analysis of motor cortex calcium activity preceding lever pulls.

claim: Activation of motor cortex starts at approximately 2 s prior to a random unrewarded left limb movement.
source: We found inhibition of motor cortex starting at approximately 5 s prior to lever pulls and activation of motor cortex starting at approximately 2 s prior to a random unrewarded left limb movement.
evidence: Supported by analysis of motor cortex calcium activity preceding spontaneous limb movements.

claim: Mice are biased toward commencing self-initiated actions during specific phases of neural activity.
source: We show that mice, like humans, are biased toward commencing self-initiated actions during specific phases of neural activity but that the pre-movement neural code changes over time in some mice and is widely distributed as behavior prediction improved when using all vs. single cortical areas.
evidence: Supported by phase analysis of neural oscillations at the time of lever pulls.

claim: The pre-movement neural code changes over time in some mice.
source: We show that mice, like humans, are biased toward commencing self-initiated actions during specific phases of neural activity but that the pre-movement neural code changes over time in some mice and is widely distributed as behavior prediction improved when using all vs. single cortical areas.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal analysis of decoding accuracy and neural dynamics.

claim: The pre-movement neural code is widely distributed as behavior prediction improved when using all vs. single cortical areas.
source: We show that mice, like humans, are biased toward commencing self-initiated actions during specific phases of neural activity but that the pre-movement neural code changes over time in some mice and is widely distributed as behavior prediction improved when using all vs. single cortical areas.
evidence: Supported by comparison of decoding accuracy using single cortical areas versus all areas.

claim: The readiness potential (RP) is a gradual increase in scalp EEG signal over pre- and supplementary motor area occurring prior to movement in humans.
source: Over the past several decades studies of volitional, that is free and voluntary, action in humans using self-initiated (i.e., uncued) behaviors such as flexing a finger or pressing a button have shown that prior to movement there is a gradual increase in scalp electroencephalography (EEG) signal over pre- and supplementary motor area (pre-SMA and SMA, respectively; Ball et al., 1999; Cunnington et al., 2002). This increase in activity is known as the 'readiness potential' (RP; Kornhuber and Deecke, 1964; Deecke et al., 1976; Deecke and Kornhuber, 1978; Libet et al., 1983; Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to established literature on the readiness potential.

claim: Human fMRI studies have shown that upcoming behaviors could be decoded up to several seconds prior to movement.
source: In parallel, human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have shown that upcoming behaviors could be decoded up to several seconds prior to movement (Soon et al., 2008; Soon et al., 2013; Bode et al., 2011; Colas and Hsieh, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to human fMRI studies on decoding voluntary behavior.

claim: Volitional actions are more likely to occur during certain phases of breathing (e.g., exhalation).
source: These debates on the neural genesis of voluntary action are further complicated as other studies have shown volitional actions are more likely to occur during certain phases of breathing (e.g., exhalation; Park et al., 2020), or phases in cumulative neural activity (i.e., the crest in slow cortical potential – SCP; Schmidt et al., 2016) which have no immediately obvious connections to volitional intent, awareness, neural noise, or external stimuli or cues.
evidence: Supported by citation to Park et al., 2020.

claim: Volitional actions are more likely to occur during phases in cumulative neural activity (i.e., the crest in slow cortical potential – SCP).
source: These debates on the neural genesis of voluntary action are further complicated as other studies have shown volitional actions are more likely to occur during certain phases of breathing (e.g., exhalation; Park et al., 2020), or phases in cumulative neural activity (i.e., the crest in slow cortical potential – SCP; Schmidt et al., 2016) which have no immediately obvious connections to volitional intent, awareness, neural noise, or external stimuli or cues.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmidt et al., 2016.

claim: Several nonhuman studies have identified structure or increases in pre-movement neural activity in nonhuman primates.
source: There is evidence to support this direction as several nonhuman studies have identified structure – or increases – in pre-movement neural activity in nonhuman primates (Romo and Schultz, 1986; Romo and Schultz, 1990; Coe et al., 2002; Lee and Assad, 2003; Maimon and Assad, 2006; Ding and Hikosaka, 2006), rodents (Hyland, 1998; Isomura et al., 2013; Murakami et al., 2014), crayfish (Kagaya and Takahata, 2010), and zebrafish (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in nonhuman primates.

claim: Several nonhuman studies have identified structure or increases in pre-movement neural activity in rodents.
source: There is evidence to support this direction as several nonhuman studies have identified structure – or increases – in pre-movement neural activity in nonhuman primates (Romo and Schultz, 1986; Romo and Schultz, 1990; Coe et al., 2002; Lee and Assad, 2003; Maimon and Assad, 2006; Ding and Hikosaka, 2006), rodents (Hyland, 1998; Isomura et al., 2013; Murakami et al., 2014), crayfish (Kagaya and Takahata, 2010), and zebrafish (Lin et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in rodents.

claim: Self-initiated behaviors in mice are preceded by an increasingly stereotyped average widefield [Ca++] signal up to 5 s or earlier in several areas including motor and limb cortex.
source: Similar to the RP in humans, self-initiated behaviors in mice are preceded by an increasingly stereotyped average widefield [Ca++] signal up to 5 s or earlier in several areas including motor and limb cortex (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: This common dynamical pattern was observed in all sessions and animals but not when considering random segments of neural activity.
source: This common dynamical pattern was observed in all sessions and animals but not when considering random segments of neural activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by comparison with random neural activity shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Four of six mice learned the lever lockout period of 3 s.
source: Four of six mice learned the lever lockout period of 3 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 shows peaks at 3 s in the inter-lever-pull intervals in mice M3–M6)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Four of six mice learned to pull increasingly more often toward the end of each ~20-min session.
source: and four of six mice learned to pull increasingly more often toward the end of each ~20-min session (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, mice).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mice tended to decrease their body movements prior to a lever pull.
source: Mice tended to decrease their body movements prior to a lever pull and we did not find evidence of stereotyped behaviors prior to lever pull (Figure 1—figure supplement 5; see also Methods on detecting stereotyped movements).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: We did not find evidence of stereotyped behaviors prior to lever pull.
source: Mice tended to decrease their body movements prior to a lever pull and we did not find evidence of stereotyped behaviors prior to lever pull (Figure 1—figure supplement 5; see also Methods on detecting stereotyped movements).
evidence: Supported by analysis described in Methods and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Upcoming rewarded lever pulls could be decoded several seconds prior to movement with decoding accuracy curves improving closer to the lever-pull time.
source: Upcoming rewarded lever pulls could be decoded several seconds prior to movement with decoding accuracy curves improving closer to the lever-pull time (examples in Figure 1h).
evidence: Supported by decoding results shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Spontaneous limb movements were also decodable above chance a few seconds prior to movement.
source: Similarly, spontaneous limb movements were also decodable above chance a few seconds prior to movement (examples in Figure 1i, j).
evidence: Supported by decoding results shown in Figure 1i, j.

claim: Pooled sessions EDTs were lower for all mice.
source: Pooled sessions EDTs were lower for all mice (Figure 2f – left panel; pvals <0.01 for all animals; single session averages in seconds: M1: −2.91; M2: −2.87; M3: −4.75; M4: −3.55; M5: −4.32; M6: −6.91; concatenated averages in seconds: M1: −4.84; M2: −5.47; M3: −7.58; M4: −5.76; M5: −6.99; M6: −6.92).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of single session versus concatenated session EDTs shown in Figure 2f.

claim: EDTs decoded from lockout trials were shorter.
source: We found that after lockout the neural data had a single negative (i.e., inhibitory) phase preceding self-initiated rewarded lever pulls that comenced ~5 s prior (similar to Figure 1e; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2). We additionally found that EDTs decoded from lockout trials were shorter (Figure 2g: average EDT in seconds: mouse 1 (M1): −1.93; M2: −3.14; M3: −2.27; M4: −1.87; M5: −1.64; M6: −2.49).
evidence: Supported by EDT analysis of lockout trials shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Low-pass filtering the neural time series (at 0.3 Hz) resulted in EDTs more similar to the initial results.
source: However, low-pass filtering the neural time series (at 0.3 Hz) (as a type of feature engineering based on power analysis results in Figure 7) resulted in EDTs more similar to the initial results (Figure 2; average EDTs of causal filtered neural data in seconds: M1: −3.5; M2: −4.85; M3: −6.95; M4: −4.31; M5: −3.0; M6: 3.7).
evidence: Supported by EDT analysis of filtered data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Somatosensory-limb cortex was generally the most informative of upcoming lever pulls (i.e., lowest mean EDTs across all mice) followed by motor cortex.
source: Somatosensory-limb cortex was generally the most informative of upcoming lever pulls (i.e., lowest mean EDTs across all mice) followed by motor cortex; visual cortex-based decoding had the highest EDTs (i.e., closest to lever-pull time t = 0 s).
evidence: Supported by comparison of EDTs across different cortical areas.

claim: Using all regions for decoding yielded lower EDTs than using somatosensory-limb cortex alone.
source: More importantly, using all regions for decoding yielded lower EDTs than using somatosensory-limb cortex alone (two sample KS test comparing limb-cortex vs. all neural regions EDTS; D-statistic for all mice: 1.0; p values: M1: 0.0; M2: 5.55e−16; M3: 2.90e−22; M4: 2.77e−19; M5:4.52e−21; M6: 2.22e−16).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of decoding using single versus all cortical areas.

claim: Across all animals, upcoming body movements could be predicted above chance a few seconds prior to movement in the vast majority of sessions and in some cases more than 10 s prior to movement.
source: Across all animals, upcoming body movements could be predicted above chance a few seconds prior to movement in the vast majority of sessions and in some cases more than 10 s prior to movement (Figure 2l).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis of body movements shown in Figure 2l.

claim: The phase distribution for a single session and cortical area was narrowly distributed with most phases falling in a <90° wide window in many sessions (and <45° for some sessions).
source: The phase distribution for a single session and cortical area was narrowly distributed with most phases falling in a <90° wide window in many sessions (and <45° for some sessions) (see Figure 3b for example distribution from phases in Figure 3a; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2 for examples from all cortical areas).
evidence: Supported by phase distribution analysis shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Random segments of neural activity had widely distributed phases.
source: In contrast, random segments of neural activity had widely distributed phases (Figure 3c, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by phase distribution analysis of random segments shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some mice had more than a 50% probability of initiating action in the crest phase – while others preferred the rising phase.
source: In contrast to human results, we found an even higher bias as some mice had more than a 50% probability of initiating action in the crest phase – while others preferred the rising phase (see Figure 3g for two examples).
evidence: Supported by phase probability analysis shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The phases for all mice, sessions, and trials showed that virtually all mice and cortical areas had narrowly distributed phases.
source: The phases for all mice, sessions, and trials showed that virtually all mice and cortical areas had narrowly distributed phases (Figure 3h) significantly different than random segments of neural activity (Figure 3i; Rayleigh test for uniformity <<1E−5 for all animals and areas).
evidence: Supported by phase distribution analysis shown in Figure 3h and statistical testing.

claim: The median inter-area phase correlation varied with some mice having highly correlated phases across areas whereas others having mostly low correlations.
source: Lastly, the median inter-area phase correlation varied with some mice having highly correlated phases across areas whereas others having mostly low correlations (Figure 3j; see also Methods).
evidence: Supported by inter-area phase correlation analysis shown in Figure 3j.

claim: Between the first and last days of the experiment three of the mice (M2, M3, and M6) increased the number of rewarded lever pulls while one additional mouse (M5) also had a positive trend (with pval of 0.13).
source: Considering the number of rewarded lever pulls per session, we found that between the first and last days of the experiment three of the mice (M2, M3, and M6) increased the number of rewarded lever pulls while one additional mouse (M5) also had a positive trend (with pval of 0.13); one of the mice (M1) decreased its number of pulls per day and the remaining mouse did not have statistically significant changes (Figure 4a; Pearson correlation values provided in figure insets; see Methods).
evidence: Supported by longitudinal analysis of lever pulls shown in Figure 4a.

claim: EDTs shortened (i.e., were closer to the lever-pull time) over time in two mice (M1 and M6); a similar trend was present in another mouse (M5; pval 0.06); while the remaining three mice did not show statistically significant trends.
source: In particular, we found that EDTs shortened (i.e., were closer to the lever-pull time) over time in two mice (M1 and M6); a similar trend was present in another mouse (M5; pval 0.06); while the remaining three mice did not show statistically significant trends.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal EDT analysis.

claim: Two mice (M1 and M6) that had decreasing EDTs (i.e., poorer decoding over time) also had an increased similarity (i.e., increased AUC values) between lever-pull dynamics and random neural states.
source: We found that, as in the EDT longitudinal trends, two mice (M1 and M6) that had decreasing EDTs (i.e., poorer decoding over time) also had an increased similarity (i.e., increased AUC values) between lever-pull dynamics and random neural states.
evidence: Supported by convex hull AUC analysis.

claim: While five of the six mice had increasing convex hulls, the trends were statistically significant in only two of the mice, which again, were mice M1 and M6 (although mouse M3 also showed a similar trend, p value: 0.14).
source: While five of the six mice had increasing convex hulls, the trends were statistically significant in only two of the mice, which again, were mice M1 and M6 (although mouse M3 also showed a similar trend, p value: 0.14) (Figure 4i).
evidence: Supported by convex hull analysis shown in Figure 4i.

claim: The overlap decreased with time in two of the mice (M4 and M6) and showed a similar trend in another mouse (M3; pval 0.09); and it increased with time in mouse M1.
source: We also found mixed results with respect to the intersection between the right paw convex hull, that is the paw used to pull the lever, and the lever-pull convex hulls: the overlap decreased with time in two of the mice (M4 and M6) and showed a similar trend in another mouse (M3; pval 0.09); and it increased with time in mouse M1.
evidence: Supported by analysis of convex hull overlap between right paw and lever pull.

claim: The variance was also stereotyped with a significant change (decrease in five mice; increase in one mouse: M2) several seconds prior to the movement-related areas (e.g., motor, somatosensory, and retrosplenial) but less so in areas not directly related to movement preparation (e.g., visual cortex).
source: Interestingly, the variance was also stereotyped with a significant change (decrease in five mice; increase in one mouse: M2) several seconds prior to the movement-related areas (e.g., motor, somatosensory, and retrosplenial) but less so in areas not directly related to movement preparation (e.g., visual cortex; Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by variance analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In mice with significant numbers of detected EVDTs (i.e., mice M3, M4, M5, and M6) the average EVDT for all areas was around −3 s or earlier.
source: While these measurements were noisy (see Methods), in mice with significant numbers of detected EVDTs (i.e., mice M3, M4, M5, and M6) the average EVDT for all areas was around −3 s or earlier.
evidence: Supported by EVDT analysis across mice.

claim: Across all animals the proportion of rewarded lever pulls compared to all other movements ranged from 0.03 (M1) to 0.07 (M2).
source: Across all animals the proportion of rewarded lever pulls compared to all other movements ranged from 0.03 (M1) to 0.07 (M2) (Figure 6c).
evidence: Supported by behavioral analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: For all animals, the intra-animal EDT distributions were not statistically different from each other when locking out licking events.
source: We found that for all animals, the intra-animal EDT distributions were not statistically different from each other (Figure 6f).
evidence: Supported by EDT analysis with licking lockout shown in Figure 6f.

claim: EDTs for two mice (M1 and M2) stayed the same, while for four mice they shortened with increasing lever-pull lockout duration (M3–M6).
source: We also recomputed EDTs for each animal and session after enforcing periods of 3–15 s of lockout (in increments of 3 s) (Figure 6g). EDTs for two mice (M1 and M2) stayed the same, while for four mice they shortened with increasing lever-pull lockout duration (M3–M6) (Figure 6g).
evidence: Supported by EDT analysis with varying lockout durations shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Average EDTs for band-passed neural data ranged from approximately −3 to −7 s.
source: We also recomputed locked-out EDTs for each animal (as in (g)) but following low-pass filtering the neural time series (filter set to 0.3 Hz; see Methods) as described above (Figure 6i). We found that average EDTs detected were longer than using non-filtered data (Figure 6j; e.g., 15-s lockout data means: M1: −3.50; M2: −4.85; M3: −6.95; M4: −5.01; M5: −3.0; M6: −3.70).
evidence: Supported by EDT analysis of filtered data shown in Figure 6j.

claim: Across all mice the vast majority of session averages had power peaks falling between 0.2 and 0.6 Hz.
source: We evaluated the peak frequency of session averages (i.e., we computed the power-spectrum-density of the lever-pull trial average for each session; ses also Methods). Across all mice the vast majority of session averages had power peaks falling between 0.2 and 0.6 Hz (Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by power spectrum analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Mouse M1 showed significant drops in power in limb, motor, and retrosplenial cortex.
source: The peak frequency power also exhibited differences between animals and also longitudinally (Figure 7d). For example, mouse M1 showed significant drops in power in limb, motor, and retrosplenial cortex, while other mice showed increases in power in limb or motor cortex (M2: limb; M3: motor; M4: motor; M6: limb).
evidence: Supported by power analysis shown in Figure 7d.

claim: Three animals had mid to strong-level increases in peak frequency (in all areas) with time (M1, M4, and M5).
source: In contrast with session averages, single-trial analysis showed more statistically significant trends (p values <0.05) in most animals and areas considered (retrosplenial, limb, and motor cortex): three animals had mid to strong-level increases in peak frequency (in all areas) with time (M1, M4, and M5); one animal (M6) had slight increases in frequency power in retrosplenial and limb cortex; and one animal has mid to strong decreases in peak frequency over time (M2) (mouse M3 had a −0.01 Pearson correlation value with time in limb cortex).
evidence: Supported by single-trial frequency analysis.

claim: We identified between 13,757 and 124,397 left paw movement bouts in individual mice.
source: Across all video recorded sessions we identified between 13,757 and 124,397 left paw movement bouts in individual mice (i.e., times where the left paw moved; see Methods; number of movements in all mice: M1: 54016; M2: 16241; M3: 18186; M4: 20487; M5: 13757; M6: 124397).
evidence: Supported by body movement tracking data.

claim: This approach revealed between 96 and 557 left paw movements that had at least 5 s of no preceding body movements and were completely isolated from lever pulls.
source: This approach revealed between 96 and 557 left paw movements that had at least 5 s of no preceding body movements and were completely isolated from lever pulls (number of movements per mouse: M1: 416, M2: 96, M3: 133, M4: 167, M5: 177, M6: 557).
evidence: Supported by analysis of isolated left paw movements.

claim: In four mice (M1, M3, M4, and M5), this signal showed a significant increase prior to movement (i.e., rising above 3× the standard deviation of the preceding neural activity) commencing approximately −2 to −1 s relative to paw movement time.
source: We computed the upper-limb cortex average signal for all animals and found that in four mice (M1, M3, M4, and M5), this signal showed a significant increase prior to movement (i.e., rising above 3× the standard deviation of the preceding neural activity) commencing approximately −2 to −1 s relative to paw movement time (Figure 8f).
evidence: Supported by neural activity analysis shown in Figure 8f.

claim: Both motor and upper-limb cortex showed a significant increase in the average neural signal beginning at approximately 2 s prior to paw movement.
source: Computing the average neural signals in motor, upper-limb, and retrosplenial cortex from the means in all mice we found that both motor and upper-limb cortex showed a significant increase in the average neural signal beginning at approximately 2 s prior to paw movement (Figure 8g).
evidence: Supported by average neural signal analysis shown in Figure 8g.

claim: The average neural signal in these areas prior to water-rewarded (locked-out) lever pulls showed a decrease commencing as early as −5 s prior to lever pull.
source: In contrast, the average neural signal in these areas prior to water-rewarded (locked-out) lever pulls showed a decrease commencing as early as −5 s prior to lever pull (Figure 8h).
evidence: Supported by neural activity analysis shown in Figure 8h.

claim: Neural mechanisms underlying self-initiated action could be preserved between mice and humans.
source: Our results also suggest that neural mechanisms underlying self-initiated action could be preserved between mice and humans.
evidence: Based on inference from similarities between mouse and human results in the study.

claim: These findings support the presence of structured multi-second neural dynamics preceding self-initiated action beyond that expected from random processes.
source: These findings support the presence of structured multi-second neural dynamics preceding self-initiated action beyond that expected from random processes.
evidence: Based on inference from the decoding and variance analysis results.

claim: Six GCaMP6 transgenic male mice (Ai93 and Ai94; Madisen et al., 2015) were used.
source: Six GCaMP6 transgenic male mice (Ai93 and Ai94; Madisen et al., 2015) were used.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental subjects used.

claim: Mice were kept on a restricted water schedule as previously described (see Silasi et al., 2016).
source: Mice were kept on a restricted water schedule as previously described (see Silasi et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental protocol with citation.

claim: Images were captured at 30 Hz with 8 × 8 pixel binning, producing a resolution of 68 µm/pixel.
source: Images were captured at 30 Hz with 8 × 8 pixel binning, producing a resolution of 68 µm/pixel (Vanni and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Direct statement of imaging parameters.
